lesson_title: Bumper Cars and Burning Grass: Reaction Rates
hook_text: Dry grass burns in seconds. An iron gate rusts over years. Both are reacting with oxygen. Why the difference?
clip_script: A veld fire and a rusting gate are the same kind of event — stuff reacting with oxygen. One takes seconds, the other takes decades. The difference is a game of bumper cars. Reactant particles are cars at a night market, bumping constantly — but a bump only COUNTS if it's hard enough and at the right angle. Chemists call the hard-enough bar the activation energy, and the counting bumps effective collisions. Every trick for speeding up chemistry rigs this game. Add more cars to the floor — that's concentration: more bumps per minute. Smash the one big car into twenty small ones — that's surface area: a boulder hides its particles inside, powder puts every particle on the floor. That's why fine maize dust can explode while a solid cob just burns. Turn up every motor — that's temperature, the strongest lever: suddenly far MORE bumps clear the bar. And the catalyst? Sneakiest of all. It doesn't touch the cars — it LOWERS the bar, opens a side gate, and never gets used up doing it. One game, five levers — and every explanation mark in the exam ends with the same six words: more effective collisions per second.
visual_style: Neon bumper-car floor where hard head-on hits flash green and glancing taps fizzle grey; levers on the wall labelled concentration, surface area, temperature, catalyst, each visibly changing the floor when pulled.
mood: Arcade energy with a clean logical payoff.
pacing: Fire-versus-rust cold open, quick game-rules beat, four rapid lever pulls, six-word closing chant.
